clue.text: Country inn's opening — what's filling it first?

indicators.note: says the filling of 'what' comes first, ahead of the word it
the filling of a word is what sits between its first and last letters, here inside 'what'

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the opening of the word inn is its first letter

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders what the stuffing is in a country inn's first dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what's filling' looks like a question about food; it is the middle of the word 'what', and 'first' sets that ahead of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caribbean republic sharing the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic is a nation.

clue.text: Landlord keeps his head, seeing composer

indicators.note: one word holds another inside it

parts.note: a host is a landlord who receives guests at an inn
the head of the landlord, the first letter of the word Landlord

explanation.surface: A pub landlord stays calm under pressure, watching a musician play.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustav Holst was the English composer of The Planets.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Holst wrote The Planets suite, so the name is that of a writer of music.

clue.text: This means beer with no head on it doesn't last

indicators.note: the beer loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: a pint is a glass of beer
something that ends does not go on lasting

explanation.surface: Someone means that a beer without froth won't keep.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter admitted the published clue was an unamended draft: 'This' is left over, and 'means' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean to do something is to plan or aim to do it.

clue.text: Home above Nag's Head one saves for landlord

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first piece sits above the next

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: the head of the word Nag's is its first letter

parts.note: a keeper, the goalkeeper, is one who saves shots

explanation.surface: A man stays home over at the Nag's Head pub, saving for the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nag's Head is a typical British pub name. 'above' puts IN before N.
explanation.definitionFit: The keeper of an inn is its proprietor, the man who runs it.

clue.text: Some stationery — no point keeping record

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: one word holding another inside it, as a keeper holds something

parts.note: a taper narrows to a point, so taper can stand for a point
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A shop sells writing paper but has no pen point to keep the record with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' is not a full stop or compass point but a taper, something that narrows to a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing paper for letters is a kind of office supply sold by stationers.

clue.text: Rose and Crown almost destroyed because of football result?

indicators.note: destroyed letters are smashed and reassembled in a new order
the last letter is missing, so the word is nearly complete

explanation.surface: Two pubs, the Rose and the Crown, are wrecked after a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims CROWN to CROW, and 'destroyed' rearranges ROSEANDCROW. The Rose and Crown is a classic British pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalless match, 0-0 in soccer, is a game ending level with neither side scoring.

clue.text: Drink makes you slightly less than stable

indicators.note: one letter short of the word, its last letter dropped

parts.note: a stable of racers or performers is a team

explanation.surface: A drink makes you a little wobbly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stable' is a noun here, a group such as a team, not an adjective meaning steady.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a hot beverage, a cuppa.

clue.text: Some drinks served up in gastropub

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letters run upwards, read from bottom to top
the letters sit inside the word gastropub

explanation.surface: Some drinks are brought to the table in a gastropub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds STROP inside 'gastropub'; 'served up' turns it to PORTS. A gastropub is a British pub serving good food.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a fortified wine from Portugal, so ports are drinks.

clue.text: Gnome to stand up and run — bravo

parts.note: a claim that stands up proves true
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
Bravo is B in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A garden gnome is urged to stand up and run, to cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' is a short saying, a maxim, not a garden ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome is a pithy saying or maxim, an aphorism.

clue.text: They placed drink under bunk

indicators.note: in a down clue, the drink goes below the other piece

parts.note: to do a bunk is British slang for to do a runner, to flee
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Someone stashes a drink under a bunk bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed' means finished in a placing, as in a race. 'Do a bunk' and 'do a runner' are British slang for running off.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who finish second in a contest are said to be placed, behind the winner.

clue.text: Excited as The Red Lion gets private party

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up and rearranged into a new order

parts.note: something private is your own

explanation.surface: Drinkers at a pub called the Red Lion get worked up when a private party is booked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excited' scrambles ASTHEREDLION into LETONESHAIRD, then OWN completes it. The Red Lion is a common British pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: To party is to relax and behave without inhibition, the idiom for abandoning restraint.

clue.text: After time, perhaps patron's round — one bitter?

indicators.note: the following pieces come after the letter for time

parts.note: an angel is a financial backer or patron, especially of a theatre production
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: After closing time a regular's round includes one pint of bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one bitter?' is not a beer: the question mark hints at a citrus fruit with sharp, bitter flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: A tart citrus hybrid of tangerine and pomelo is a sharp-tasting fruit, so loosely one bitter thing.

clue.text: If he's drunk, you get distorted vision?

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of order, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: If he has been drinking, his eyesight goes blurred.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a wide-angle lens gives a warped view rather than literally faulty eyesight.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide-angle photographic lens bends the image, giving a warped, bulging view.

clue.text: No doubt about clubs in 16 getting repossession order

indicators.note: the first word goes round the others

parts.note: for sure means certainly, without doubt

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the band's name

parts.note: 16 across is a band, and ELO, the Electric Light Orchestra, is one
C is the card abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Golf clubs at a band's venue are definitely seized by the bailiffs.
explanation.walkthrough: '16' points to the answer at 16 across, a band, standing in for one particular band, the Electric Light Orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: A lender's legal action to take back a mortgaged property is a seizure ruling.

clue.text: Hide expensive as case for one's iPhone accessory?

indicators.note: the first word acts as a case round the others, holding them inside it

parts.note: dear means costly or expensive
one is I, and 's is the contraction of is
an app is a program added to a smartphone such as an iPhone

explanation.surface: A pricey phone case is sold as an accessory for an iPhone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' is a verb here, not an animal skin or a birdwatcher's shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: To hide is to vanish from sight, the verb sense meaning go out of view.

clue.text: Control freak goes around middle of pub giving talks

parts.note: a dial is a control knob

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go round the middle letter
used as a verb, to freak is to go wild, so the letters are rearranged
the middle letter of the word pub

explanation.surface: An obsessive person wanders round the pub, lecturing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freak' looks like a noun in 'control freak' but rearranges GOES as OGES; 'around' puts it round U, the 'middle of' pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialogues are conversations, exchanges of words.

clue.text: Cricketer's house next door to Black Bull

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
BS is short for bullshit, slang for nonsense or bull

explanation.surface: A cricketer lives next door to a pub called the Black Bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cricketer's' means 'cricketer is'. Jack Hobbs was a great England batsman of the early twentieth century; cricket is a bat-and-ball sport played in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Jack Hobbs was a celebrated English batsman, so the name stands for a sportsman of that game.

clue.text: Gets intoxicated before seeing area around Inverness

indicators.note: the second word goes before the first

parts.note: high means drunk or intoxicated
to land something is to get it

explanation.surface: Someone gets drunk before visiting northern Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Inverness is the main city of the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish Highlands is the mountainous northern region whose capital is Inverness.

clue.text: Old woman repulsed by half-empty beer's colour

indicators.note: repulsed means pushed back, so the word is turned round

parts.note: one's old woman is slang for one's mother, ma
the beer is half emptied inside: of its two middle letters only one is left

explanation.surface: A mother is disgusted by a half-drunk glass of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repulsed' turns MA into AM. 'half-empty' does not halve the word: just one of the two inner Es goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is a golden yellow-brown shade, a hue like many beers.

clue.text: White Horse regular fills tankard

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another, filling it

parts.note: a beaker is a large drinking cup, like a tankard
R is an abbreviation for regular

explanation.surface: A regular at the White Horse pub fills his tankard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White Horse' is not a pub: white horses are white-crested waves at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A white-capped wave breaking at sea is called a white horse.

clue.text: Band wants to be great and mature — whiskey's refused

parts.note: to rock is slang for to be excellent

indicators.note: the letter is turned away and taken out

parts.note: to grow up is to mature
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A band of musicians wants to grow up, so they turn down the whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refused' removes W from GROW UP.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical group playing loud guitar-based music is a band.

clue.text: This time some drinkers want port

definitions.meaning: the moment the pub's doors are unlocked for business, eagerly awaited by thirsty drinkers
a port is a hole or gap, as a porthole is in a ship

explanation.definitionFit: Pubs announce when they unlock, a time drinkers await; a port is a gap or aperture.

clue.text: Popular pub's entrance blocked? How disappointing was the manager?

indicators.note: the first letter, the way in, is shut off and removed

parts.note: the Rovers Return is the pub in the long-running British TV soap Coronation Street
aw is an exclamation of disappointment

explanation.surface: A busy pub's door is barred, and the manager is not impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rovers Return is the pub in Coronation Street, a long-running British TV soap. 'entrance blocked' drops its R.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee is to supervise, the job of a boss, so oversaw means supervised.

clue.text: A dram's about right for this

definitions.text: A dram's about right for this

indicators.note: the word goes round the letter

parts.note: a shot is a dram of spirits

explanation.surface: A tot of whisky is just the thing here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts R inside SHOT. As a whole, a dram is a small measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A small measure of spirits is called this in pubs, a single serving of whisky.

clue.text: It's crude to get very drunk?

definitions.text: It's crude to get very drunk?

parts.words: It's crude to get very drunk?
parts.note: a drilled source from which petroleum is extracted, with very drunk hinting at the phrase well oiled

explanation.surface: Getting plastered is a rather vulgar thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crude' looks like 'vulgar' but means crude oil; 'very drunk' is the slang 'well-oiled' turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A bored shaft from which petroleum is pumped is where crude is extracted.

clue.text: Musician sees off pub's first band

indicators.note: to see off is to get rid of, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a player is a musician

indicators.note: the first letter of pub's is the one taken

explanation.surface: A musician leaves the pub's first band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sees off' removes the first letter of pub's, P.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is a band or stratum, as in rock.

clue.text: Now new designer has it in UK, NY sent out secret agent?

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the scrambled letters
the letters are dispatched in different directions and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Mary Quant was the British fashion designer famed for the miniskirt
taken as written

explanation.surface: A new designer brings her label to Britain while New York sends out a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent out' rearranges UKNY as UNK...Y. Mary Quant was a British fashion designer. 'secret agent?' is a person whose nature is hidden, not a spy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose abilities or intentions nobody knows is a mystery, an agent whose qualities are secret.

clue.text: Throw up a lot of wine — what's the point?

indicators.note: in a down clue, the word is thrown upwards and read from bottom

parts.note: a bin is a stock of wine, as in a bin end

explanation.surface: Someone vomits after a lot of wine and asks why bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what's the point?' is a question about purpose on the surface; a pen's tip is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A nib is the writing tip of a pen.

clue.text: Wine's vintage, regular admits, is no secret

indicators.note: one word lets the other in, holding it inside

parts.note: stable means steady or regular
cru is a French term for a vineyard or wine of a particular growth

explanation.surface: A regular drinker admits the vintage of a wine is common knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is no secret' reads as a verb phrase; 'is' is a link, and 'no secret' is an adjective-like phrase meaning understandable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open to understanding or interpretation is not hidden, the opposite of inscrutable.

clue.text: Let us be taunted about addition to 5

indicators.note: each word is turned around in its place

parts.note: taken as written
to rag is to tease or taunt

explanation.surface: Someone invites mockery by stirring something into the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns US to SU and RAG to GAR. 5 refers to the answer at 5 down, a hot drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetener spooned into a cuppa is something added to it.
